editorial:
The Virginian (Paramount, 1929) is a sound Western directed by Victor Fleming from a screenplay by Edward E. Paramore Jr. and Howard Estabrook, adapting Owen Wister's 1902 novel and the 1904 Wisterâ€“La Shelle stage play. Gary Cooper, in his first starring Western and first sound film, plays the unnamed Virginian opposite Walter Huston as the villain Trampas; Richard Arlen and Mary Brian round out the leads. It was the third screen adaptation of Wister's story â€” silent versions appeared in 1914 and 1923 â€” and the first with spoken dialogue. The 1929 print, together with its original recorded soundtrack and both Wister source works, entered the public domain in the United States on January 1, 2025, ninety-five years after release. For a creator, that means raw footage, stills, and the dialogue itself are all free to quote, sample, re-edit, or redistribute without a licence.

The rights trap is the restoration, not the term. By the 1960s surviving exhibition prints had deteriorated badly in both picture and audio quality. In the 1990s the UCLA Film & Television Archive restored the film as part of its Paramount collection preservation programme, and any print or digital master derived from that work carries a modern copyright distinct from the 1929 film's status. Commercial home video editions almost certainly draw from the UCLA master. A creator who wants to use footage without restriction must verify that the specific copy in hand predates or is independent of that restoration â€” an unrestored archival duplicate struck from a pre-1990s element falls outside the restoration claim, but anything sourced from the UCLA master does not.
faq: Is the 1929 Virginian in the public domain?

The 1929 Paramount print and its original recorded soundtrack entered the public domain in the United States on January 1, 2025, ninety-five years after release. The underlying Owen Wister novel (1902) and stage play (1904) are also long in the public domain. That status does not extend to the UCLA Film & Television Archive's 1990s restoration of the film, which carries its own modern copyright; commercial home video editions almost certainly derive from that restored element and are not free to use.
Can I use footage from a DVD, Blu-ray, or streaming copy of The Virginian?

Probably not freely. Commercial home video releases of this film almost certainly derive from the UCLA Film & Television Archive restoration rather than an unrestored archival print, and that restoration is separately copyrighted. To use footage without restriction you need to verify that the specific copy you are working from predates or is provably independent of the 1990s restoration. When the provenance is unclear, contact the UCLA Film & Television Archive directly before publishing.
